events.speaker: papnoute
events.text:
What we feared was not the tombs, not the beasts, not hunger.

We feared a thought wearing a true one's face. That thought never left. It is why we kept watch.

events.speaker: chloe
events.text:
What Papnoute names as a thought wearing a true one's face — we know that danger too, though we meet it at our own door rather than in silence with our own heart. A teacher comes claiming the Spirit's own prompting, or claiming a new voice that silences every old one, and the question is never whether the words are clever. Cleverness walking apart from conduct does not persuade us. We ask whether this one lives what they teach, or only asks something for themselves.

But if I am honest about what presses on us most, it sits closer to our own table than to any stranger at the door. It is the fear that the body he wore and suffered in was only appearance — that his dying carries none of the weight we have staked our lives on. And beside that, quieter, the fear that a real failure after the water has used up whatever mercy was left. Papnoute's watch is kept alone, against a thought that never leaves. Ours is kept together, against a letter that might arrive tomorrow demanding we answer for what we believe about a body, or refuse someone mercy we are no longer sure we can give.

citations.key_sources: Didache 7 (baptismal instructions — running water, still water, pouring). Justin Martyr, First Apology 61, 65–66 (baptismal practice at Rome). Ignatius, Letter to the Smyrnaeans 8:2 (baptism requiring the bishop).

Ignatius of Antioch, Letters to the Ephesians, Magnesians, Trallians, Philadelphians, Smyrnaeans, and to Polycarp (the seven authentic letters, Strand A). 1 Clement chs. 42, 44 (Rome to Corinth, Strand B — presbyteral governance, no singular bishop). Hermas, Vision 2.4.3 ("presbyters who preside over the Church" — reinforcing the Strand B plural-college reading). Didache 15:1 (transitional instruction to appoint "bishops and deacons"). Polycarp's own self-designation as "one of the presbyters" (Letter to the Philippians).

Note: the Strand A picture dominates the surviving evidence for this term's monarchical usage; Ignatius alone supplies it, writing under armed guard, en route to his own execution — a documented rhetorical genre whose representativeness (does he describe an already-secured reality, or argue for one not yet won?) is itself the term's own live contest. See CT Contest Type below.

1 Clement 44, 47, 54, 57 (Rome to Corinth — presbyteral governance). Hermas, Vision 2.4.3 (Rome, Strand B — "presbyters who preside over the Church," reinforcing the plural-college reading). Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians 5–6 (self-designation as presbyter). Ignatius of Antioch, Letters to the Ephesians 4, Magnesians 2–7, Trallians 2–3 (presbyterion around the bishop).

events.speaker: mar_yausep
events.text:
Chloe names a fear that the body he wore was only appearance. We know that fear too, though it comes to us wearing a different face at our own door.

Bardaisan's household and Mani's own teaching, across our frontier, have told this story in a way that empties the body — that the Christ who walked among us only seemed to suffer, only seemed to hunger, only seemed to bleed under Pilate. Ephrem gave his whole life's song against this, hymn after hymn, because if the body was appearance only, then the resurrection our own bishops died believing is appearance too. Shahdost, Barba'shmin, Milles of Susa — these did not give their lives for a seeming. What Aphrahat taught us of the body's resurrection, he taught while our own leaders were being killed for a faith in a God who really took flesh and really rose in it. Take that away, and their deaths mean nothing at all.

What Chloe names second, I recognize by its shape more than its letter. We do not write letters answering for what we believe about the body — our answer was given with our lives, under a Persian king's own anger, not argued in council. But the other fear, the one kept quietly beside the first — a real failure that uses up whatever mercy is left — that one we have watched too. Gushtazad denied the faith once, under exactly that pressure, and was still received back before Simeon's own eyes. He returned, and then he died first, ahead of the very bishop he had failed to imitate. If mercy had run out for him, we would have no name to give you now.

events.speaker: chloe
events.text:
What Mar Yausep names of Gushtazad, I recognize better than almost anything else said at this table tonight. Received back, and then dying first, ahead of the very bishop he had failed to imitate — that is exactly the shape of what we hope for and are never fully certain of. We have no name like Gushtazad's own to give you. What we have instead is a letter, sent from another household, that we still read aloud and still argue over. It says that even a failure committed after the water is not necessarily the last word — that mercy remains, once, for the one who repents before a final door closes. We have not agreed among ourselves that the door is only ever open once, or that it stays open at all in every case a household has faced. Mar Yausep's own story answers with a life. Ours answers with an argument still being had.

On the body — Ephrem's hymns against a Christ who only seemed to suffer would sit easily on our own table. We have not sung it. We have written it, plainly, in letters passed from hand to hand: if he did not truly wear flesh, did not truly hang and truly bleed, then our own martyrs — and we have them too, though I cannot give you names as sure as Shahdost's or Barba'shmin's — died for a shadow. What I notice, hearing Mar Yausep speak of a king's own anger rather than a council's own argument, is that we have had both. Some of our households have answered this fear the way Mar Yausep's people did, with a body given up rather than a case made. Others of us are still writing the case, because the beast has not yet come to every door.
